INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE 1
Founded in 1893, the International Association of
Chiefs of Police (IACP) is the world’s largest
professional association of law enforcement leaders, with
more than 35,000 members across over 180 countries.  In
the United States, IACP’s members include police
chiefs, sheriffs, superintendents, and other commandlevel officials who lead agencies of every size, from small,
rural departments, to state police agencies, to the
Nation’s largest metropolitan forces.  IACP seeks to
advance the interests of police and promote
professionalism in policing through advocacy, research,
education, and the development of model policies and
standards.
Promoting officer safety is central to IACP’s mission.
IACP’s members are the officials responsible for
deciding how officers are trained and equipped to
respond when an armed attacker opens fire.  For more
than three decades, IACP has concluded that AR-15
platform and similar semiautomatic rifles pose a distinct
threat to officers and the public.  In 1992, IACP’s
membership adopted a resolution calling for a
prohibition on such weapons.  In 2003, it adopted a
resolution strongly supporting reauthorization of the
federal assault weapons law before its scheduled 2004
expiration, along with technical amendments to
strengthen it.  After the law expired, IACP urged law

1 Pursuant to this Court’s Rule 37.6, amicus  states that no counsel
for any party authored this brief in whole or in part, and that no
person or entity other than amicus, its members, or its counsel made
a monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation or

2

enforcement leaders to advocate for its reinstatement.
In 2009, IACP again formally supported legislation to
reinstate these restrictions, citing officer safety, gang
and drug-trafficking violence, and the growing criminal
use of such firearms.  And IACP reaffirmed its
longstanding support for these restrictions in a 2018
position paper. 2  IACP’s members took each of these
actions because, as law enforcement leaders, they
understand that the criminal use of AR-15 platform and
similar semiautomatic rifles poses an increased risk both
to officers and to the communities they are sworn to
protect.
In these cases, the Court is being asked whether to
strike down two state and local laws prohibiting the
possession of AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic
rifles.  IACP submits this brief in hopes that, in
answering this question, the Court will consider the
perspective of the law enforcement officers who must
confront these weapons each day.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Every day, in small towns and big cities across the
country, law enforcement officers risk their lives to
protect their communities.  It is their job to run toward
danger, especially when no one else can or will.  Most of
them do so carrying a pistol—typically in 9mm, 10mm,
or .40 or .45 caliber—and wearing a soft body armor vest

2 See Int’l Ass’n of Chiefs of Police, Firearms Policy Position
Statement (2018), https://www.theiacp.org/sites/default/files/2019-
05/IACP%20Firearms%20Position%20Paper_2018%20(1).pdf.

3

suitable for protecting against handguns—equipment
that has saved the lives of thousands of officers.
But when the danger is a shooter armed with a
semiautomatic rifle like an AR-15, neither is enough.
The rounds from those rifles can penetrate the vest, and
the shooter can hit officers from distances their pistols
cannot reach.  In short, the officers are outgunned.  That
reality means that officers face an increased risk of death
and serious injury in the line of duty, as recent incidents
in Charlotte, North Carolina and elsewhere across the
country tragically illustrate.  In light of such incidents,
police chiefs nationwide have raised the alarm that,
when officers are outgunned, those officers, as well as
the communities they are sworn to protect, are less safe.
The outcome of these cases could shape that reality for
years to come.
Although the threat that AR-15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles pose to police is national in scope,
the right response may vary from state to state.
Different states may reasonably reach different
judgments about whether to keep these rifles out of
circulation altogether, prohibit carrying them in
crowded public spaces, or limit who can acquire them.
Some states may prefer to invest in equipment and
training better suited to dealing with the risks posed by
these weapons.  That flexibility, under which states
implement the solutions that best match their needs,
derives from our constitutional order.  It properly leaves
the facets of governing that most directly touch citizens’
daily lives, like the prevention of crime, to “smaller
governments closer to the governed.”  NFIB v. Sebelius,

4

567 U.S. 519, 536 (2012) (opinion of Roberts, C.J.).
Amicus asks the Court, in deciding these cases, to
remain mindful of the officers who will live with the
consequences of its decision and to preserve room for
states and their law enforcement agencies to work
together on solutions suited to their own circumstances.
ARGUMENT
I. AR-15 Platform and Similar Semiautomatic
Rifles Leave Officers Tasked With Protecting
the Public Outgunned.
1.  Each day in the United States, hundreds of
thousands of law enforcement officers leave their homes
not knowing whether they will return.  They knock on
doors behind which armed suspects may wait.  They
approach cars on dark roadsides with no way of seeing
what the driver has within reach.  And when gunfire
erupts in a school or supermarket, or on a crowded
street, they move toward it while others seek cover.
This Court has long recognized these dangers:
“American criminals have a long tradition of armed
violence, and every year in this country many law
enforcement officers are killed in the line of duty, and
thousands more are wounded.”  Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S.
1, 23 (1968).  It has also recognized that officers cannot
avoid that danger by standing back: “The role of a peace
officer includes preventing violence and restoring order,
not simply rendering first aid to casualties.”  Brigham
City v. Stuart, 547 U.S. 398, 406 (2006).
Amicus’s members are the officials responsible for

5

protecting the officers tasked with carrying out those
duties.  To that end, police departments across the
country provide their officers with equipment designed
to meet the threats they most commonly face.  By 1997,
98% of officers nationwide were authorized to carry
semiautomatic handguns. 3  Likewise, by 2013, 82% of
officers were “required … to wear protective armor at
all times.”4  First developed in the 1970s, the “soft body
armor” that most officers wear today is composed of a
“ballistic-resistant,” “lightweight fabric” designed for
day-to-day use.5  And such armor has been enormously
effective: “[T]he risk of fatality for officers assaulted
with a firearm while not wearing body armor was 14
times higher than for officers wearing body armor.” 6
Indeed, by one count, such armor had by 2014 prevented

over 3,100 officer fatalities nationwide.7
2.  When a suspect is armed with an AR-15 platform
or similar semiautomatic rifle, the calculus changes
entirely.
To begin, an officer’s handgun is no match for an AR-
15 platform rifle.  These rifles are ordinarily chambered
for much more powerful ammunition: AR-15 platform
rifles fire intermediate rifle cartridges that can exit the
muzzle at roughly 3,200 feet per second—more than
2.5 times the exit velocity of a 9mm pistol—and they
strike their targets with over three times the kinetic
energy.  JA101.  AR-15-style rifles are also accurate at
far greater distances.  Such weapons have an effective
range of 400 to 500 yards, while a typical handgun’s is
about 50.  Id.  Imagine an officer taking fire from five
football fields away, yet she can only return fire at half
of one football field—just one tenth of the distance
needed to defend herself.  An officer in this situation may
have no way of effectively returning fire on the shooter.
In such circumstances, the features that make the 9mm
well suited to the close-range encounters that dominate
day-to-day policework offer little help.  With their
extensive training and experience, officers are well
equipped to hold their own against suspects armed with

Law Enforcement Officers When It Matters Most: Hearing Before
the S. Comm. on the Judiciary , 113th Cong. 2 (2014) (statement of
Sen. Patrick Leahy, Chairman), https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/

14LeahyStatement.pdf (last visited Oct. 27, 2026).

7

handguns, shotguns, or knives.  But training cannot close
the firepower gap for the officer facing a well-positioned
criminal armed with an AR-15 platform or similar
semiautomatic rifle.
There is more.  Compounding the risk is the fact that
standard-issue lightweight body armor was not
designed to stop the bullets fired by AR-15-style rifles.
Soft body armor was specifically created to protect
against bullets fired from “ handguns.”8  As such, the
more powerful rounds fired by an AR-15-style weapon
“can travel through most soft body armor and standard
protective equipment used by law enforcement.”  JA42.
And the risk of serious injury or death to officers
carrying and wearing standard-issue equipment is
exacerbated by other “combat-functional” features of
AR-15-style weapons, H.R. Rep. No. 103-489, at 18
(1994), that petitioners themselves acknowledge.  For
example, such weapons are designed to have “little
recoil,” which makes them “accurate,” “easy to shoot,”
and “user friendly.”  Pet. Br. 9 (citation omitted).
Beyond that, features of these weapons, such as pistol
grips and high-capacity, detachable magazines,
“increase[] stability” and “control[].”  JA136.  Petitioners
also recognize that these features “can result in more
effective shot placement … and require less time to
acquire successive targets.”  Id.; see also H.R. Rep. No.
103-489, at 19 (noting that the high-capacity magazines
accepted by AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic

8 Criminal Justice Tech. Testing & Evaluation Ctr., Body Armor
Overview & History, supra note 5 (emphasis added).

8

rifles “make it possible to fire a large number of rounds
without re-loading, then to reload quickly when those
rounds are spent”).
AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles
therefore pose a combination of dangers not shared by
any other weapon that officers commonly encounter in
the field.  A bolt-action rifle, such as those traditionally
used for hunting, may fire a more powerful round over
long distances, but it must be manually cycled between
shots.  A handgun can be fired rapidly, but its rounds are
the ones patrol armor is built to stop, and it is effective
only at close range.  AR-15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles pair range and armor-defeating
power with sustained, accurate, rapid fire.  That
combination allows a single shooter to accurately target
officers with multiple rounds capable of piercing officers’
vests—from a distance that prevents officers armed
with handguns from effectively returning fire.
3.  An example illustrates the real-world implications
for officers.  At around 1:30 p.m. on April 29, 2024, a joint
fugitive task force led by the U.S. Marshals Service and
the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department (CMPD)
arrived at a house in east Charlotte, North Carolina, to
serve a warrant on a convicted felon wanted for
unlawfully possessing a firearm. 9  The subject “saw the

accordingly—taking his “AR-15-style rifle” with him to

approached, they were “immediately met with gunfire”
from above. 12  The ensuing standoff lasted for three

responding to the scene.14

Officers Sam Poloche and William Elliott of the North
Carolina Department of Adult Correction; and Deputy
U.S. Marshal Thomas Weeks. 15  Officer Eyer—who had
recently been named CMPD’s “officer of the month”—
“was killed while responding to others who were facing

The outcome turned on the weapon involved.  As
then-CMPD Chief of Police Johnny Jennings explained
after the attack, because the shooter was armed with an
AR-15-style rifle, he was able to “unload several rounds
towards [the] officers within [a] matter of seconds”—
rounds that “the traditional body armor for police
officers does not withstand.” 17  That situation, Chief
Jennings went on to state, presented responding officers
with “dangers that most humans should not have to
face.”18  The officers faced those dangers heroically,
doing everything their training and their oaths
demanded of them.  “[N]ot a single one of them backed
away.”19  Still, four of them did not come home.
4.  Charlotte was not an isolated incident.  To the
contrary, in recent years, stories of officers being killed
by individuals with AR-15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles have become sadly commonplace.
To take just a few further examples:
Douglas County, CO.   In the early morning of
December 31, 2017, officers responding to a 911 call
found an individual barricaded inside his room. 20  After

5.  In the wake of these tragedies, law enforcement
leaders nationwide have sounded a common refrain: AR-
15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles place police
officers in greater danger.35
The experience of the Nation’s officers is borne out
by the data.  According to one study from 2018, AR-15
platform and similar semiautomatic rifles account for

II. States and Their Law Enforcement Agencies Need
Flexibility to Protect the Officers Who Protect
Them.
Departments and their chiefs across the country
must reckon with these weapons, but the threat they
pose may look different from one state to the next.
Amicus submits that, although the problem identified in
this brief is national in scope, the solution may vary from
state to state.  In amicus’s view, state legislatures—
rather than localities acting via ordinance or bylaw—are
best positioned to strike that balance on a statewide
basis, calibrating their responses to conditions within
their borders while sparing officers and law-abiding
citizens alike a confusing patchwork of rules that
changes from one municipal boundary to the next.
According to data compiled by the Federal Bureau of
Investigation, in 2025, 37% of law enforcement officers
nationwide worked in states that restricted the
distribution or possession of AR-15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles in some form.38  A decision from this

States, 572 U.S. 844, 854 (2014).  And so, because “[i]t
goes without saying that preventing and dealing with
crime is much more the business of the States than it is
of the Federal Government,” this Court has said that it
does “not lightly construe the Constitution so as to
intrude upon the administration of justice by the
individual States.”  Patterson v. New York, 432 U.S. 197,
201 (1977).  Though Patterson addressed a different
question, its teaching holds true here too: decisions
about how best to protect the officers who stand
between the public and violent crime lie at the very
heart of the administration of justice, and they are best
made by those closest to it.
Amicus’s request is a simple one.  It asks this Court,
in deciding these cases, to remain mindful of the officers
who will live with the consequences of that decision, and
of the need to permit states and the law enforcement
professionals who serve them to work together to
implement solutions tailored to their unique
circumstances.  The officers who answer calls, approach
doors, and run toward gunfire do so on behalf of the
communities they serve.  States should have a voice in
how those officers are protected.
